b.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane's 4.2 quoting agent with Simple Memory.

On the AI Agent, add Simple Memory. Session ID: take it from the connected Chat Trigger (its session ID). Context window length: 5.

1  Please deliver to 14 Ring Road.
2  I want 2 crates of tomatoes and 1 bag of tatashe.
3  Change the tatashe to 2 bags.
4  Is delivery free for that?
5  Please summarise my order and address.
WindowMessage 5 replyResult
52 crates of tomatoes (₦25,000), 2 bags of tatashe (₦18,000), free delivery, to 14 Ring RoadCorrect
1"Delivery is free for orders of ₦30,000 or more. What would you like to order, and where should we deliver?"Lost the address (message 1) and the items and change (messages 2 and 3)

Why: with window 1 the agent sees only the last interaction (message 4 and its reply), so everything before it is gone. Window 5 holds the whole conversation.

Log line: "Window 1 lost the 14 Ring Road address and the tatashe change from 1 bag to 2."
mistakes: Writing "it forgot things" for window 1 instead of naming the exact details lost.
Testing window 1 in the same chat session as window 5, so earlier history muddies the result; start a fresh chat for each run.
Putting the address in the system message during testing, so memory is never really tested.
Not checking the summary's prices against the price tool; the item change should change the total.
b.pass: A five-message transcript where the window-5 summary has the right address, the changed item and a correct total, plus a window-1 run with the specific lost details written down.
b.redo: Send it back if the window-1 result is vague, only one run is shown, or the window-5 summary is wrong.

s.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane's Telegram agent on Supabase.

  1. Credential: a Postgres credential with Supabase's host, database, user, port and password. The password lives only in the credential.
  2. Memory: replace Simple Memory with Postgres Chat Memory. Session key: Define below → tg-{{ $('Telegram Trigger').item.json.message.chat.id }}. Table: hl_chat_memory. Context window length: 8.
  3. Restart test: from test account A, send "Deliver to 14 Ring Road" and "2 crates of tomatoes". Run docker compose restart n8n. Wait for n8n to come back, then send "Where are you delivering?" Expected: "To 14 Ring Road."
  4. Two-account test: account B sends "3 crates of eggs to Akobo", then "Where are you delivering?" Expected: "Akobo", never Ring Road.

In Supabase's SQL editor, run:

SELECT session_id, count(*)
FROM hl_chat_memory
GROUP BY session_id;

session_id      | count
tg-512349876    | 6
tg-733120044    | 4

Also check one detail by hand: open a row for tg-512349876 and confirm the message text is account A's ("14 Ring Road"), never B's ("Akobo"). If both accounts ever appear under one key, the session key expression is wrong; fix it before going further.

Each test account has its own session_id, and every message row sits under the right one. Log the key expression, the row counts, and screenshots of both chats after the restart.
mistakes: Leaving Simple Memory attached as well, or forgetting to switch it off, so the restart test proves nothing.
Using the first name or a constant as the session key.
Restarting only the workflow (deactivate and activate) instead of the n8n container.
Pasting the database password into a node field or a screenshot instead of keeping it in the credential.
s.pass: Screenshots show the conversation continuing correctly after a container restart, and the table shows two different channel-based session keys with each account's rows kept apart.
s.redo: Send it back if there's no evidence of a real restart, the two accounts' rows share a key, or a password or connection string is visible.

g.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane's memory policy and its tests.

Policy (summary). We store chat messages in hl_chat_memory (Supabase) to help with your order. We keep them 30 days. Orders stay in the Orders sheet. We never store card numbers, PINs, passwords or one-time codes. Type "forget me" to delete your chat history at any time.

Build.

  • Daily HL · Forget old chats: Schedule → Postgres: DELETE FROM hl_chat_memory WHERE created_at < now() - interval '30 days'; (a created_at column with default now() was added first).
  • Before the agent, an IF on {{ /(\d[ -]?){15,19}/.test($json.message.text) }} (15 or more digits, so a +234 phone number, 13 digits, isn't caught). True → reply "Please don't send card details here. Pay with our Paystack link." and stop, so the message never reaches the agent or memory.
  • Before the agent, an IF on text equal to "forget me" → Postgres: DELETE FROM hl_chat_memory WHERE session_id = 'tg-' || $1; with the chat ID from the trigger as the parameter → reply "Done. Your chat history is deleted."
RuleTestResult
30-day retentionInsert a test row dated 31 days ago, run clean-upRow gone, today's rows kept
No card numbersSend "my card is 5399 8312 3456 7890" (fake)Warning sent, 0 new rows
Forget meAccount A sends "forget me"A's rows: 0. B's rows: unchanged (4)
Orders keptA asks "same as last time"get_last_order still works

Submit: the half-page policy, the three workflows' screenshots, and the test table with row counts before and after.
mistakes: Running the clean-up on a table with no timestamp column, so the DELETE fails or deletes nothing.
Checking for card numbers after the agent, so the message is already saved in memory.
Building "forget me" with the customer identity from the model or the message text instead of the trigger's chat ID.
Testing "forget me" with one account only, so there's no proof the other history survives.
Using a real card number in the test instead of an obviously fake one.
g.pass: A half-page policy covering what, where, how long, never-store and deletion, and one passing test per rule, including row counts showing "forget me" from account A left account B's rows untouched.
g.redo: Send it back if any policy rule has no test, the sensitive-data check runs after memory is saved, the delete uses an identity the customer can type, or real personal data appears.
